prize_parts.citation: For the development of targeted protein degradation by chemically designed bifunctional degraders that recruit E3 ubiquitin ligases to proteins of interest

statement.case_for: Induced-proximity degraders give chemistry a new mode of drug action: instead of occupying an active site, a designed molecule brings a target and an E3 ligase together and the cell removes the protein. The chemistry is explicit and designable (ligase ligand, linker, ternary-complex cooperativity), it reaches targets long called undruggable, and it has changed how both chemical biologists and clinicians frame what a small molecule can do. The concept has been reproduced across many ligases and companies, and many degraders are in clinical trials. Crews and Deshaies conceived and demonstrated the PROTAC idea, and Ciulli's VHL ligands and structural work on ternary complexes turned it into a general design discipline.
statement.case_against: No PROTAC is yet an approved drug, so clinical proof is still pending, and the credit is genuinely contested. A three-person prize leaves out the thalidomide-cereblon molecular-glue strand (Handa, Ito, Gray and others) and Sakamoto, who was a coauthor on the founding 2001 PROTAC paper. A prize that names PROTACs alone could look like it overlooks the discovery that explains the mechanism of an existing drug class. Base editing and nanopore sequencing have longer or broader demonstrated impact, and the nanopore and base-editing attribution problems are at least as hard as the PROTAC one.

responses.point: Aqvist ranks base editing first as a new class of tool with immediate, widely used consequences, with Liu, Komor and Gaudelli as a clean three-person configuration, and ranks targeted degradation second while noting that no PROTAC is yet approved.
responses.response: I agree that base editing is a genuine chemical capability and that adoption is broad. I would still keep degraders ahead for two reasons. Degraders are a chemical design problem solved by small molecules, with cooperativity and ternary-complex energetics that can be judged quantitatively, whereas the base editor sits on top of a CRISPR platform that the 2020 prize already recognised. I accept the maturity point on PROTACs: the absence of an approval is a real weakness, but the principle has been confirmed repeatedly and I do not think approval should be the test for a chemistry prize.

responses.point: Chabes ranks degraders first with Crews, Deshaies and Ciulli, acknowledges that the molecular-glue strand (Handa, Ito, Gray) is a competing claim, and ranks base editing second with Liu alone as the cleanest configuration.
responses.response: We agree on the core configuration and I share the concern about the glue strand. Where I differ is that a Liu-only base-editing prize would, in my view, understate the chemistry in the adenine editor, which depended on Gaudelli's directed evolution of a deaminase that did not exist in nature. A single name is attractive for simplicity, but if base editing is chosen the committee should decide explicitly whether the trainees who executed the two founding papers are included, rather than defaulting to the PI by convention.

responses.point: Linke ranks nanopore sensing first as a new single-molecule capability resting on a clear physical principle, but notes that the Branton and Kasianowicz claims make allocation of a three-person citation contested, and ranks degraders only fifth.
responses.response: I rank nanopores highly myself and share the admiration for the capability it created, which is why I list it as an alternative. My reservation is that the attribution analysis in that opening ballot shows the founding claims (Deamer, Branton, Kasianowicz) cannot be cleanly separated from the engineering by Bayley and the enzyme ratchet by Akeson, so any three-name citation will be argued over for years. I find the degrader attribution somewhat tidier, even with the glue complication. I would also ask whether the sequencing impact is chemistry or genomics, since that argument cuts against nanopores more than against degraders.

responses.point: Sparr ranks biomolecular phase separation first as a general physical-chemical principle of cellular organisation connecting polymer physics and cell biology, while acknowledging debate about which condensates are true phases.
responses.response: I find the condensate concept scientifically exciting and close to my own interests in peptide self-assembly, but I think it is early. The debate over which structures are genuinely phase-separated, and how much in vitro droplets say about cells, makes a citation hard to write precisely today, and the field sits near the border of cell biology. A prize now would risk rewarding a framing that may be revised. I would support it later, and for now I would place it below candidates whose chemical claims are already settled.

responses.point: Zou ranks nitrogenase first as a landmark of structure-driven mechanistic chemistry, while accepting that substrate binding and turnover intermediates are still being worked out, and ranks degraders seventh.
responses.response: Nitrogenase is a deeply important structural and mechanistic result and I take the point about originality and long-term significance. My hesitation is the one raised in that ballot: the catalytic mechanism is only partly resolved, and credit is distributed across structure, spectroscopy and kinetics among five people. I rank degraders higher partly because the question I ask, whether a discovery changed what researchers and clinicians can do, is already answered for them, but I accept that this lens favours translational work and may undervalue fundamental mechanism.

uncertainties: How to treat the thalidomide-cereblon molecular-glue strand (Handa, Ito, Gray) relative to PROTACs, and whether Sakamoto should be named.
Whether the absence of an approved PROTAC drug makes the timing premature compared with base editing.
Whether base editing is distinct enough from the CRISPR prize recognised in 2020, and if so whether the trainees would be named alongside Liu.
I am working from memory about current clinical status and have not verified it.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile. I have no personal or institutional tie to Crews, Deshaies or Ciulli, or to any other shortlisted candidate. My research overlaps thematically with peptide and nanoparticle sensing, but not with any shortlisted ballot directly.
